name: Puzzle
description: Clear rules, a hand-tuned difficulty curve and plenty of polish. Small systems, lots of content.

pillars.name: Aha Moments
pillars.feeling: the solution clicks, and I feel clever

pillars.name: One Idea at a Time
pillars.feeling: each puzzle teaches or twists one thing
pillars.rulesOut: puzzles that pile on everything at once

gameExamples.heading: Pitch
gameExamples.text: A calm puzzle game of short, hand-made levels, each built around one clear rule twist.

gameExamples.heading: Core Loop
gameExamples.text:
1. Look at the board.
2. Try moves and undo freely.
3. Spot the trick and solve it.
4. Unlock the next puzzle.

gameExamples.heading: Non-goals
gameExamples.text:
- Timers and fail states.
- Random puzzles.

docs.title: Core Rules
docs.summary: The puzzle's logic as the player sees it: what's allowed, and how a puzzle is won or lost.

examples.heading: The Player Can
examples.text:
- As a player, I can understand every rule from what's on screen.
- As a player, I can try a move and see its result.

examples.heading: The Player Sees
examples.text: - Pieces that show what they can do.

examples.heading: Rules
examples.text:
- No hidden rules.
- Every puzzle has at least one solution.

docs.title: Board Logic
docs.summary: The board state, moves, and checking for a solution.

examples.heading: How It Works
examples.text: The board is a grid of cells holding pieces. A move is validated, applied, and pushed onto an undo stack; after each move the win check runs.

examples.heading: Code
examples.text:
- `UBoardState`: cells, pieces and moves
- `UMoveValidator`: checks moves against the rules
- `UUndoStack`: stores board snapshots

examples.heading: Data
examples.text: - Board size and piece types per level.

docs.title: Puzzle Pieces
docs.summary: Piece and board meshes or sprites, and their move and match effects.

examples.heading: Assets Needed

examples.heading: Style
examples.text: Simple, tactile pieces with one color per piece type and soft lighting.

examples.heading: What to Look For
examples.text:
- Minimal 3D or 2D puzzle packs.
- Satisfying UI sound packs (clicks, pops).

examples.heading: What to Avoid
examples.text: - Detailed textures that distract from shapes.

docs.title: Puzzles
docs.summary: The puzzles themselves and the order they come in.

examples.heading: The Player Can
examples.text:
- As a player, I can play puzzles in a set order.
- As a player, I can skip back to any solved puzzle.

examples.heading: The Player Sees
examples.text: - A level select with solved and unsolved puzzles.

examples.heading: Rules
examples.text: - Each world introduces one new mechanic.

docs.title: Difficulty Curve
docs.summary: Introducing ideas one at a time and combining them later.

examples.heading: The Player Can
examples.text:
- As a player, I can learn a new mechanic in an easy puzzle first.
- As a player, I can face harder combinations later.

examples.heading: The Player Sees
examples.text: - Optional hard puzzles marked as such.

examples.heading: Rules
examples.text:
- Each mechanic gets a teaching puzzle.
- Difficulty dips after every hard puzzle.

docs.title: Level Data
docs.summary: How puzzles are authored, stored and loaded.

examples.heading: How It Works
examples.text: Each puzzle is a data asset with the board layout and the par number of moves. A level editor writes these assets.

examples.heading: Code
examples.text:
- `UPuzzleLevel`: data asset per puzzle
- `UPuzzleEditorWidget`: editor tool for authoring puzzles

examples.heading: Data
examples.text: - Puzzle levels as data assets.

docs.title: Puzzle Levels
docs.summary: The list of puzzles and the data asset for each.

examples.heading: Assets Needed
examples.text:
| Asset | Type | Status | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Puzzle level data | Data | Placeholder | To source |
| World backgrounds | Mesh | Placeholder | To source |

examples.heading: Style
examples.text: Each world has its own calm palette.

examples.heading: What to Look For
examples.text: - Background packs with soft gradients.

examples.heading: What to Avoid
examples.text: - Busy backgrounds behind the board.

docs.title: Hints and Undo
docs.summary: Helping stuck players without giving the answer away: undo, restart and hints.

examples.heading: The Player Can
examples.text:
- As a player, I can undo any number of moves.
- As a player, I can ask for a hint when stuck.

examples.heading: The Player Sees
examples.text:
- An undo button always visible.
- Hints that point at a piece, not the solution.

examples.heading: Rules
examples.text:
- Undo is unlimited.
- A hint is available after a minute stuck.

docs.title: Meta Progression
docs.summary: Stars, unlocks and other reasons to keep going between puzzles.

examples.heading: The Player Can
examples.text:
- As a player, I can unlock new options between runs or levels.
- As a player, I can see what I can unlock next.
- As a player, I can choose what to work toward.

examples.heading: The Player Sees
examples.text:
- An unlock screen with locked and unlocked items.
- Progress bars toward the next unlock.

examples.heading: Rules
examples.text:
- Unlocks add options, not raw power.
- Everything can be unlocked by playing.

docs.title: UI
docs.summary: Menus and HUD: what the player sees and can do outside the game world.

examples.heading: The Player Can
examples.text:
- As a player, I can start, pause and quit from clear menus.
- As a player, I can change graphics, audio and control settings.
- As a player, I can see the information I need during play without it covering the action.

examples.heading: The Player Sees
examples.text:
- A title screen, pause menu and settings screens.
- A HUD with only what matters right now.
- Button prompts that match my input device.

examples.heading: Rules
examples.text:
- Every screen can be used with a gamepad as well as mouse and keyboard.
- Pausing stops gameplay time.
- Settings save immediately.

docs.title: UI Framework
docs.summary: How screens and widgets are built, opened, navigated and fed data.

examples.heading: How It Works
examples.text: Screens are UMG widgets pushed onto a stack by a UI manager subsystem. The top screen gets input; popping it returns to the one below. Gameplay talks to the HUD through events, never directly.

examples.heading: Code
examples.text:
- `UProjectUISubsystem`: owns the screen stack and opens and closes screens
- `UScreenWidget`: base class for every full screen (menus, settings)
- `UHUDWidget`: the in-game HUD; listens to gameplay events

examples.heading: Data
examples.text:
- Screen classes and their input modes in a data asset.
- Settings in the game user settings, saved per user.

docs.summary: Icons, fonts, panels and widget skins.

examples.heading: Style
examples.text: Clean and readable first: flat shapes, high contrast, one accent color. Icons share one line weight and perspective.

examples.heading: What to Look For
examples.text:
- UI kits with matching icons, buttons and panels.
- Fonts licensed for games, with the character sets we localize to.
- Input prompt packs covering keyboard, Xbox and PlayStation.

examples.heading: What to Avoid
examples.text:
- Mixing icon packs with different styles.
- Ornate frames that crowd the screen.
- Fonts that are hard to read at small sizes.

docs.title: Music and Sound
docs.summary: Music, sound effects and ambience, and where each is used.

examples.heading: Assets Needed
examples.text:
| Asset | Type | Status | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Main theme | Music | Placeholder | To source |
| Gameplay loops | Music | Placeholder | To source |
| UI sounds (click, back, confirm) | Sound | Placeholder | To source |
| Ambience beds | Sound | Placeholder | To source |

examples.heading: Style
examples.text: Music sets the mood of each area; sound effects are short and punchy so they read over the music.

examples.heading: What to Look For
examples.text:
- Music packs with loopable stems.
- Sound effect libraries with variations of each sound.
- Licenses that allow commercial use and streaming.

examples.heading: What to Avoid
examples.text:
- Tracks that don't loop cleanly.
- Effects with long tails that muddy fast moments.
- Mixing many libraries with different loudness.

docs.title: Save and Load
docs.summary: Which puzzles are solved, and the player's settings.

examples.heading: How It Works
examples.text: A save game object holds everything that persists. Systems register what they need saved; saving serializes it to a slot, loading restores it before the level starts. Saves carry a version number so old saves can be migrated.

examples.heading: Code
examples.text:
- `USaveSubsystem`: saves and loads slots, runs migrations
- `UProjectSaveGame`: the saved data, with a version field
- `ISaveable`: interface for systems that write and read their part

examples.heading: Data
examples.text:
- Save slots in the platform's save location.
- A version number per save, bumped on every breaking change.
